title: Hundreds of Masked White Nationalists Marched Through Washington on America's 250th Birthday. They Chanted 'Reclaim America.'
excerpt: The Patriot Front's flash-mob march near the US Capitol came hours after Trump called immigrants a 'communist menace' at Mount Rushmore — a jarring backdrop for the 4.8 million Indian Americans celebrating the Fourth of July.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Hundreds of masked white nationalists marched in D.C. on America's 250th birthday.
  • The Patriot Front's demonstration coincided with Trump's anti-immigrant rhetoric.
  • Indian Americans celebrated Independence Day amid rising nativist sentiments.
  • No arrests were made during the march, despite its hate group classification.
  • Severe weather disrupted July 4 festivities in Washington, D.C.
A Divided Independence Day
›Patriot Front marchers chanted 'Reclaim America' in D.C.
›Trump labeled immigrants as a 'communist menace' hours before the march.
›4.8 million Indian Americans celebrated July 4th amidst rising tensions.
›No arrests reported despite the march's hate group ties.
Sources: Reuters, USA Today, Southern Poverty Law Center

On the day America turned 250, hundreds of masked white nationalists marched through the streets of its capital.

Members of the Patriot Front — a white supremacist organisation founded after the deadly 2017 Charlottesville 'Unite the Right' rally — descended on Washington, D.C. on Saturday morning in a flash-mob-style demonstration. Reuters photographers captured hundreds of men in the group's signature uniform — khaki trousers, blue shirts, white face coverings, and caps emblazoned with the Patriot Front logo — riding the D.C. Metro and marching near the U.S. Capitol building.

They carried Confederate flags, inverted American flags, and the group's own banners. They chanted "Reclaim America" as they beat drums and marched past Union Station and through the Eastern Market neighbourhood, one of the closest areas to the Capitol.

The group claimed on its Telegram channel that approximately 400 members had arrived in the capital. By midday, the marchers boarded Metro trains and dispersed to New Carrollton, Maryland, in Washington's northeast suburbs.

A Jarring Counterpoint to a National Celebration

The march unfolded as millions of Americans prepared for fireworks, parades, and barbecues to mark the semiquincentennial — and as President Donald Trump readied a campaign-style rally on a fenced-off National Mall that he had billed as "the most spectacular TRUMP RALLY of them all."

The timing was not coincidental. Just hours earlier, Trump had addressed a crowd at Mount Rushmore in South Dakota, calling on Americans to protect their freedoms against what he described as a "communist menace" — rhetoric he tied directly to immigrants.

> "They chanted "Reclaim America" as they beat drums and marched past Union Station and through the Eastern Market neighbourhood, one of the closest areas to the Capitol."

"There is now a resurgence of the communist menace in our land, including from newcomers to our country who embrace ideas totally opposed to our way of life," Trump said on Friday evening, adding: "We're not going to let this happen."

At one point, the president said the "newcomers" needed to be "expelled." The choice of language — on the eve of Independence Day, at a monument carved on land sacred to the Lakota Sioux — drew sharp criticism from immigrant advocacy groups and civil rights organisations.

The Metropolitan Police responded with restraint

The Metropolitan Police Department in Washington said it had been "tracking First Amendment activities that occurred this morning in the Eastern Market neighbourhood." In a statement to reporters, the MPD said: "MPD recognises the rights of individuals to peacefully express their views and remains committed to maintaining public safety and security for DC residents and visitors."

National Guard members were also observed near the march route. No arrests were reported.

The Patriot Front is classified as a hate group by the Southern Poverty Law Center. Its manifesto states that "democracy has failed this once great nation" and calls for a "hard reset" to return to "the traditions and virtues of our forefathers" — identifying them explicitly as European settlers.

In June 2022, over 30 members, including the group's founder Thomas Rousseau, were arrested in Idaho on charges of conspiracy to riot at a Pride parade. The group was later ordered to pay Black saxophonist Charles Murrell III $2.7 million after members assaulted him during a march in Boston.

What the Diaspora Needs to Know

For the estimated 4.8 million Indian Americans in the United States, the march was a visceral reminder that the promise of belonging in America remains contested.

The Patriot Front's ideology explicitly centres white European heritage as the foundation of American identity — a framework that excludes South Asian, African, Latino, and other immigrant communities by design. Its calls to "reclaim" America echo a strain of nativist politics that has gained visibility since 2016, even as Indian Americans have emerged as one of the fastest-growing and most influential diaspora communities in the country.

The march came on a day when Indian-American families across the country were celebrating the Fourth of July like any other American family — grilling in their backyards, watching fireworks with their children, and flying the flag. Community leaders noted the dissonance.

"On the day we celebrate the ideals of liberty and equality, we saw armed men in masks march through our capital chanting to reclaim an America they believe belongs only to them," said one Indian American advocacy group's statement shared on social media. "We will not be erased."

The broader context is equally unsettling. Trump's Mount Rushmore speech framing immigrants as a "communist menace" was his most pointed conflation of anti-communist and anti-immigrant rhetoric to date, coming as progressive Democratic candidates won primary elections across several states.

A Celebration Interrupted by Weather — and Ideology

By late afternoon, Washington's July 4 festivities were disrupted not by protests but by weather. Severe thunderstorms forced the evacuation of the National Mall celebration, with Secret Service ordering thousands to seek shelter. Lightning was visible near the Washington Monument as dark clouds rolled in, and the Freedom 250 event was temporarily halted.

Confusion reigned as some in the crowd ignored evacuation orders, chanting "USA" and booing when told to leave a second time.

The storms eventually passed, and Trump's evening rally and fireworks display proceeded — but the image of masked white nationalists marching through the capital on America's birthday was already seared into the day's history.

*Sources: Reuters, USA Today, New York Post, The Times (UK), Southern Poverty Law Center*
